And when three cells had burned,

Now, concerning this capture of Edessa, the holy Mor Dionysius Bar Salibi wrote two metrical homilies,
and also Mor Basil of Edessa itself [wrote] three metrical homilies,
all of them in the meter of Mor Jacob.
And when Zengi had taken Edessa,
he went and encamped against Birehjik (al-Bira),
which is a rebellious fortress overlooking the Euphrates.
And when he pressed it with battle,
news reached him of the dissension that had broken out in Mosul,
and that his deputy there, Nasir al-Din, had been killed.
Then he abandoned it and returned to Mosul.
Now the Franks who were in Birehjik,
because they feared lest Zengi return against them,
sent to Husam al-Din Timurtash, son of Ilghazi, son of Artuq, lord of Mardin,
and surrendered it to him.
He, however, [Timurtash son of] Ilghazi, fearing lest Zengi march up against his territory
and subdue his fortresses,
and through them gain mastery over his entire domain,
demolished most of the fortresses that belonged to him:
that of Khur'bar {OCR?}, and that of Tel-Besme,
and that of Thuma,
and that of Tel-Shih,
and that which was near the monastery of Mor Hananya, which is called 'of the Woman'.
And at that time this Timurtash took the fortress of Hatakh from a certain Kurd,
after he had encamped against it for a year and four months,
yet through oaths, and gold, and villages that he gave to the Kurd, its owner.
And Arslan Doghmish son of Dawud, lord of Hisn Ziyad, departed from Zengi
and encamped against Tel-Arsenios (Tel-Arsenyas?),
and demanded that they surrender it;
but they were unwilling,
because their sons were hostages in Hisn Ziyad.
And when he waged battle against it, he quickly captured it.
And about fifteen thousand souls were found in it,
refugees from the whole region.
And he commanded,
and all of them, together with their bishop Timothy,
became slaves
and were sold.
And in the year one thousand four hundred and fifty-six [of the Greeks],
540 of the Arabs (AH),
Zengi sent an army against the fortress of Fanak, which is beside the island of Qardu (Jazirat Ibn 'Umar),
which is called 'of the Sons of 'Umar'.
This was an impregnable fortress that overlooked the Tigris,
and it had been in the hands of the Bashnawiyya Kurds for a period of three hundred years.
